name: Northern Guiyang Hmong
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Northern Guiyang Hmong is not in the catalog. The only stress-keyword title Glottolog attaches to it, Kan Hua (1980) on voiced/voiceless initials in Amdo Tibetan vs stressed/unstressed syllables in Old Tibetan, is a false link: the Glottolog reference page states the languoid was a 'computerized assignment from \"zhuo\"' out of LaPolla's Tibeto-Burman bibliography. It is about a Tibeto-Burman language, priority none. No first-hand statement on word stress in Northern Guiyang Hmong was found in any open source: the ISO 639-3 change request (fetched sources) names the descriptive sources (Wang Fushi 1985 Miaoyu jianzhi; Wang & Mao 1995), none online; Ratliff 2010 (sealang) is a 404; A Speech Prosody 2012 paper on Mo Piu tone (a variety only tentatively assigned to Guiyang Miao, subdialect unspecified) was fetched sources and is silent on stress. Files with.

earlier_scan.source_named: Wang Fushi (1985). Miaoyu jianzhi [A sketch of the Miao language]; Niederer (1998) Les langues Hmong-Mjen — dialect phonologies plausibly covering Guiyang Miao prosody; not online.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, Geneviève. 2012. Towards the Mo Piu tonal system: first results on an undocumented South-Asian language. Speech Prosody 2012. doi:10.21437/speechprosody.2012-33
sources.note: Mo Piu (Vietnam) is only tentatively a Guiyang Miao variety (subdialect unspecified, per Ly & Vittrant 2014 as cited by Wikipedia); the paper is about tone labelling; 0 hits for stress/accent/prominence/Guiyang.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2007. Change Request 2007-115: [huj] Hmong, Northern Guiyang -> add name Miao, Northern Guiyang. SIL International.
sources.note: Administrative only; sources cited are Hattaway 2000, Wang & Mao 1995, Wang 1985, Enwall 1994-95.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page nort1545 (Northern Guiyang Hmong)
sources.note: Only Niederer 1998 and Johnson 2002 (subclassification) and Ethnologue; 0 descriptive references.

sources.citation: 王辅世 Wang Fushi (ed.). 1985. 苗语简志 [A sketch of the Miao language]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe. (full scan, archive.org/details/20220317_20220317_1109)
sources.note: Nothing for this variety. The book's phonology chapter treats Dananshan (Chuanqiandian proper) with sketches of Layiping and Yanghao; the Guiyang subdialect appears only in the distribution list (p.104: 北部土语 ~60,000 speakers, Guiyang city outskirts, Pingba Linka, Qianxi, Jinsha, Zhenning, Kaiyang, Xiuwen, Guiding) and as the comparison point 摆托 Baituo, Qingyan, Guiyang (p.135 '摆托 (贵阳次方言的代表点, 在贵阳市青岩)'; p.140) in the lexical/grammatical comparison. scanned has 0 hits for 重音/轻读/重读/轻重; the only 轻声 remark (p.12) concerns Xiangxi (Layiping) prefixes. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Purnell, Herbert C. (ed.). 1972. Miao and Yao linguistic studies: selected articles in Chinese (transl. Chang Yü-hung & Chu Kwo-ray). Data Paper 88. Ithaca: Cornell SEAP. Contains Miao Language Team 1962 'A brief description of the Miao language' and Ying Lin / Miao Language Team 'Chinese loanwords in Miao'.
sources.note: Pai t'o (摆托), Ch'ing yen, Kweiyang City is datapoint 5 'Kweiyang subdialect' (p.56 fn.1) in 'Chinese loanwords in Miao', with tone-numbered Pai t'o forms in the loan charts; the 'brief description' says the Kweiyang subdialect has three subdivisions. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the volume. Silent.

sources.citation: CQVIP (维普) search-result pages, 14 queries (摆托/青岩/花溪/贵阳 北部土语/贵阳次方言 音系/贵阳 轻声/摆省/平岩/杨勤盛/贵阳周边地区/修文/开阳/金沙/林卡 苗语), each holding record titles and abstracts
sources.note: Bibliographic records + abstracts only. Guiyang-subdialect records: 杨勤盛 2010 苗语贵阳次方言与川黔滇次方言语音比较 (贵州民族学院学报 2010(5):97-100; abstract = sound correspondences, nothing on stress); 王辅世 & 刘援朝 1993 贵州紫云界牌苗语的语音特点和方言归属 (语言研究 1993(1); abstract names 贵阳市青岩 as the Northern-vernacular representative point); 李云兵 1993 黔西县铁石苗语语音研究 (NW vernacular, not huj); 摆省苗语音系及其语音特点 (三峡论坛; Baisheng on the Longli/Guiyang/Huishui border, affiliation unresolved). No abstract mentions 重音 or 轻声 for any Guiyang variety.
